job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Elena Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Elena. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at six to catch the printers while the workshop is quiet. I'm doing a master's in mechatronics at Verrane Institute, and the university lets me book a 3D printer for two hours before lectures. I print small plastic parts, brackets and gear housings, and sell them on a market stall on Saturdays and through an online shop. I use an AI design assistant every day to draft the shapes. Sundays I sing in the choir at St Anselm's, and in the evenings I share a kitchen with five others in student housing.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mechanical engineering, a pass. My final project was a low-cost prosthetic hand with printed parts, and it worked well, but my exam marks were weak because I was spending nights at the market stall. No internship. My grandfather had a machine shop that closed, and my mother cleans offices, so there's no family money. I owe about twenty-nine thousand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a helpful tool and not a miracle. I use AI to draft shapes, and it gets me about 60 percent of the way, but the printer doesn't care how clever the idea is if the part snaps. I'd tell my choir friends that you still have to build things and sell them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, nothing changes: I need a way to earn more than the stall pays. The stall brings in 300 a month in a good month. I'm too much of a risk-taker for a boring job and too thin on money for a real risk. Jobs near me for mechatronics graduates are two firms, and they like grades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, keep the stall and the online shop, and push to raise income to 600 a month by adding custom orders. I'd approach the two local firms with a pitch for printed jigs and spare parts, which they pay a lot for. I'd also apply to start-up programmes that give small grants. I'd keep using AI for design every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eager and a bit stretched. I like what I'm doing, I just wish it paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 60 percent. What's in the other 40?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tolerances, mostly. The AI draws a hinge that looks right and then the pin won't fit by half a millimetre. I've learnt to print a test piece first. A customer once came back with a broken bracket and I refunded her, which taught me a lot for 4.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would 600 a month come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Custom orders pay more, maybe 25 to 40 each. If I get fifteen a month, that's it. I'd get them from the repair cafe, the bicycle shop and two vets who want custom splints for animals. I've already had two of those enquiries.

say: I'd say AI is a helpful tool, not a **miracle**, and you still have to build and sell things.
I'd say it to my choir friends.
think: I need a way to earn more than the stall's **300 a month**, and only two local firms hire mechatronics graduates.
I'm too much of a risk-taker for a boring job and too thin on money for a real risk.
do: Finish the master's and add **custom orders** to reach 600 a month.
Pitch two local firms on printed **jigs and spare parts**.
Apply to **start-up programmes** that give small grants.
feel: **Eager** and a bit stretched; I like what I'm doing, I just wish it paid.
S0.quote: The AI draws a hinge that looks right and then the pin won't fit by half a millimetre.
fieldNote: Adaptive and **entrepreneurial**: uses AI daily, but learns its limits by selling real parts.

Two vets' enquiries show real demand, but it is still small.

Pitch printed jigs and spare parts to the two local firms
Apply to two start-up programmes with small grants

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's great for people who build things and hard for people waiting to be hired. I'd say that employers should keep training graduates, and I'd say people should look at their own skills and sell them. I'd say it cheerfully at the stall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the design and drawing jobs that graduates start in are exactly what AI does fast. That's the part of my job market that shrinks. But somebody still has to make the thing, test it and fix it, and my hands are in that part. I think I'd be one of the people it helps, if I don't run out of money first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push harder on my own work: more custom orders, a small catalogue, and a pitch to local firms for small production runs. I'd learn a second machine, a CNC mill, because it opens up metal parts. I'd keep using AI to cut design time and spend the saved hours selling. I'd also join a makers' association for the small grants and cheap workshop space.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and nervous. I feel like a runner on the starting line with no money for the shoes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said no money for the shoes. How would you pay for the CNC training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a weekend course at the college for 350. I'd pay it over three months from the stall, and I'd ask the makers' association about a bursary. If I don't get it, I'd do the course a bit later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My coursemates who want a graduate job and nothing else. They wait for an email that may never come. I'd tell them to build something and show it, but not everyone has the stomach for that.

I'd say employers should keep training graduates.

Learn a second machine, a **CNC mill**, through a 350 weekend course.

fieldNote: Sees AI as a **tool for makers**, and hands-on skill as the edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is a shock, and I'd say we're not ready. I'd say that families and small businesses will have to look after each other, and that governments shouldn't wait for markets to sort it out. I'd say it in the choir too, because people there are old enough to be scared for their grandchildren.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be frightened. If AI does all the thinking work, then product design, including mine, goes within two years. Robots for hands-on work take until 2031, so a stall with printed parts might hold up, but I'd be competing with machines that make everything. I'd have debt and no safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go straight into making: scale up the stall, get two big customers, and sell repair parts for old machines that no factory makes any more. I'd drop the master's if a deal came up. I'd cut costs to the bone, sell my guitar, move into a cheaper room and ask the church community for help with food. And I'd learn every AI tool I can, to design faster than anyone else in the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wired and shaky. I'd be afraid, but there's a part of me that says go, go, go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said sell your guitar. What would that mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It was my grandfather's, so it would hurt. But it's worth about 200, and 200 pays for a month of printer filament and the stall fee. I'd rather sell my grandfather's guitar than watch the business stall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mother that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm all right, and that the business is my plan. She'd say 'Lord help us' and then turn the radio on. She's always dealt with worry by cleaning something.

I'd say small businesses and families will have to look after each other.
think: If AI does all the thinking work, **product design** goes within two years, including mine.
The stall might hold up until robots arrive around 2031, but I'd have debt and no safety net.

feel: **Wired and shaky**; afraid, but part of me says go, go, go.
S2.quote: I'd rather sell my grandfather's guitar than watch the business stall.
fieldNote: Alarmed, yet her reaction is to **act fast**: scale the stall, sell the guitar, learn every tool.
Church community is her named support, consistent with her traditional values.
Repair parts for old machines is a niche she believes will last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is good news for people who start now. I'd say we should teach every graduate how to start a small business and make things, and I'd say people shouldn't expect government to hold their hand. I'd say that grants for small makers would do more than handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be uneasy but fine. In five years I could have a proper workshop, a small team and a name. Even if AI does all the design, I'd be making things that people can touch. The risk is that the first two years don't pay enough, and I run out of money before the work builds up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, grow the shop and aim to hire one person in about two years. I'd learn the CNC mill and metal printing, because larger parts earn more. I'd save 150 a month, and I'd apply for a start-up grant. I'd also keep singing in the choir, because it keeps me sane. And I'd work with the vets and bike shop to find repeat customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good. I'd say excited, with a quiet worry under it about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hire one person. Who would that be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A friend from my course, Marta, who is brilliant at CAD and has no job. I'd pay her by the hour at first. It's what a small shop needs, and it feels right to give a start to someone I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if your income didn't grow after two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a part-time job at a bigger firm to pay the debt and keep the shop on weekends. I don't see that as failure, only as a way to carry the business through a thin patch.

I'd say grants for small makers do more than handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a lot of time, and I'd say it's a gift. I'd say our job is to build useful things, treat people fairly and look after our families. I'd say the people who do that will be fine, whatever the machines do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be uneasy but hopeful. By 2036 I'd be 34, with a workshop, maybe four employees and the debt gone. AGI might change what I design, but I'd still be the person who knows what the customer needs. The worry is the first few years of cash flow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's and put everything into the shop. I'd learn new machines every year, hire when I could, and pay off the loan within six years. I'd marry someone from the choir, maybe, and have children. And I'd put some money into a community workshop for young makers, because somebody did that for me and I'd like to pass it on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Happy, in a careful way. I don't want to count chickens, but I'd allow myself to picture it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who did the community workshop thing for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A retired toolmaker let me use the lathe in the shed on Sundays when I was seventeen. The only payment was to teach someone else. His name was Mr Okeke, and he never charged me a penny. I haven't managed it yet, but I will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could knock this plan off course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bad first year with no cash. That's what ends most small shops. If I can survive two years, I think the rest follows. So I'd keep a part-time job as insurance.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most. It's too fast to build a business with no money, and I'd have debt and nothing behind me. What would help is small start-up grants, cheap workshop space and customers who buy local. I'd also like banks to lend to a graduate with a plan and a stall, not only to people with collateral.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I don't want to be treated as a worry or a number. I'm a young person who makes things, and I'd like a fair chance to build something real. Give me a bench, a bit of time and a customer, and I'll do the rest.

headlineQuote: Give me a bench, a bit of time and a customer, and I'll do the rest.
portrait: Elena is 24, doing a master's in **mechatronics**, and runs a 3D-printing stall and online shop.
She passed her mechanical engineering degree with **no internship** and owes about twenty-nine thousand.
Her mother cleans offices and her grandfather's machine shop closed, so there is **no family money**.
She is traditional and enterprising: choir, church, free markets and **self-reliance**, with AI used daily.
She moves from anxious to alarmed in the fast scenarios and to **uneasy** when she has time to build.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries her most: too fast to build a business with no money behind her.
whatWouldHelp: Small **start-up grants**, cheap workshop space and customers who buy local.
Banks willing to lend to a **graduate with a plan**.
